criteria.descriptor: Correctly separates true overfitting (train >> held-out gap) from an over-optimistic validation estimate; accurately describes leakage, improper-split, and drift/train-serving-skew mechanisms; and correctly states what L2 regularization can and cannot fix. No false claims such as 'regularization or a simpler model fixes leakage/drift' or 'a random holdout is the honest split for temporal data.'

Names at least two distinct, plausible root causes for the CV-to-production drop, each with a detection method; explains why regularization is the wrong first move; and includes a concrete re-validation/backtest plan. Full marks require all three elements plus a way to distinguish causes.

Justifies the diagnosis from the specific evidence (high CV yet low production), reasons about why each remedy does or does not address each cause, and supplies a triage/discrimination strategy instead of asserting a single cause without evidence.

Reads as a clear, prioritized design-review response using correct terminology (generalization gap, data/target leakage, time-based split/GroupKFold, covariate/concept shift, train-serving skew) and states recommended actions in a logical order.

expected_answer_points: Recognizes that a high CV score with a large production drop is not classic overfitting, because overfitting to the training set would already depress the held-out CV score; the real issue is that the CV estimate is over-optimistic relative to the deployment distribution (a generalization-estimate gap).

Explains why stronger L2 regularization is unlikely to fix this: regularization reduces variance/fitting to training noise but does nothing for leakage, bad splits, distribution shift, or train-serving skew, which are the probable causes when CV itself is inflated.
Identifies target/data leakage as a root cause and gives a concrete detection method (audit feature timing/provenance relative to the prediction cutoff; ablate suspect features and watch CV fall).
Identifies an improper CV split (random k-fold on temporal or per-customer/grouped data leaking across folds) and prescribes a time-based/walk-forward split and/or GroupKFold to re-estimate honestly.

Identifies distribution shift/concept drift or train-serving skew as a cause and gives a detection method (compare offline vs live feature distributions via PSI/KS, log serving-time features to compare against the offline pipeline).

Provides a way to distinguish the hypotheses rather than guessing one (e.g., feature-timing audit and ablation for leakage, re-run with an honest split, offline-vs-online feature comparison for shift/skew).
Specifies a validation plan: re-estimate with a leakage-free, temporally honest holdout/backtest that mimics deployment so the offline number tracks production, then confirm on live data and monitor.
common_pitfalls: Accepts the author's 'overfitting' label at face value and just recommends more L2, a simpler model, or more data, missing that a high CV score already rules out ordinary train-set overfitting as the cause.
Conflates overfitting with the CV-to-production gap, not realizing that overfitting to the training set would have depressed the CV score itself.
Names only one cause (e.g., 'it's drift') without proposing how to distinguish it from leakage or a flawed validation split.
Proposes fixes but no honest re-validation or backtest, leaving no way to confirm the offline estimate now reflects the deployment distribution.
Recommends a random k-fold or random holdout as the remedy, reintroducing the same cross-fold leakage for temporally ordered or per-customer data.
Claims regularization or reducing model complexity will fix data leakage or distribution shift, which it will not.
reference_answer:
The key observation is that the 0.93 came from cross-validation, not merely the training set. Classic overfitting means fitting training noise and generalizing poorly to held-out data, but that would already depress the CV score. Here the held-out CV estimate is high and only production is low, so the CV estimate itself is over-optimistic relative to the deployment distribution. That is a generalization-estimate problem, not high variance against the training set. Stronger L2 regularization is therefore unlikely to help: regularization trades a little bias for less variance and curbs fitting to training noise, but it does nothing about leakage, an unrepresentative validation split, distribution shift, or train-serving skew, which are the likely culprits when CV itself is inflated.

Plausible root causes and how I'd distinguish them:

1) Target/data leakage. A feature may encode the label or use post-outcome information (e.g., an account-status flag or 'days since retention call' updated at the moment of churn). Detection: audit each feature's provenance and the time it becomes available relative to the prediction cutoff; ablate suspicious features and watch whether CV falls toward the production number. Leakage is the prime suspect for a suspiciously high CV.

2) Improper CV split. Random 5-fold on temporally ordered or per-customer data leaks across folds (the future, or the same customer, appears in both train and validation), inflating CV. Fix: use a time-based/walk-forward split and GroupKFold on customer id, then re-estimate.

3) Distribution shift or train-serving skew. The live population or churn behavior may differ from the training window (covariate/label shift), or features may be computed differently online vs offline. Detection: compare offline vs live feature distributions (PSI/KS tests) and log serving-time feature values to compare against the offline pipeline.

I'd triage in that order, since a bad split or leakage could explain the whole gap by itself. To validate any fix, I'd re-estimate with a leakage-free, temporally honest holdout that mimics deployment (train on months 1..N, test on N+1); a trustworthy offline AUC should land near the 0.71 we observed and then rise only as I remove genuine problems. I'd confirm on the next month of live data and add ongoing monitoring so the offline estimate keeps tracking production.
